Introduction
Crowds are increasing rapidly, especially in developing cities (UN, 2017).Therefore,
space requirements in urban centers have become an important problem and designers
havetriedtocreatenewareas.Theneedforspaceinurbancentersisnowanimportant
problem,causingdesignerstotrytoformulatenewareas.Intheimplementationofthese
changes,basicdesigndecisionsandtheneedsofhumanpsychology,aswellastheimpor-
tanceofvisualaspectsofthecity,havebeenignored,thusleadingtomonotony.There-
fore,theresultingbadurbanizationwillgiverisetosituationswhichwillmakeitdifficult
for the individual to turn to the city, to discover the city.
The physical environment is shaped, whereby people’s movements take place and
inter-spatial relations shape the representation of the environment in the human
mind, which in turn affects the goal of reaching the desired objective (Erkan, 2017).
This action is, in a sense, wayfinding seen as an act of decision-making. In addition to

dealingwiththeproblemofgraspingthespace,people’sperceptionoftheenvironment
as a path and the junction is the cause of topological relation complexity.
These complex and topological problems have brought about many consequences in
urbanlife.Despitevarioussociologicalreasons,themovementofpeoplefromoneplace
to another in urban life is believed to rise in line with these increasing complexities,
because this action (wayfinding) is about the correct use of time, which is one of the
most valuable phenomena for people today. Urban wayfinding can be defined as the
achievement of an objective point or the directing of behavior in the physical environ-
ment. Erkan (2018) stated that many stimuli, together with physical and social factors,
affect wayfinding behavior. The topography, signs, property boundaries, and the road
layout in the environment experienced by people are critical environmental data for
shaping (Davies and Pederson, 2001; Hölscher et al., 2009; Carlson et al., 2010;
Wolbers and Hegarty, 2010). On the other hand, Lynch (1960), one of the initiators of
the concept of urban orientation, discovered the means of finding: maps, street
numbers, router signs, and other elements. From a different point of view, Passini
(1984) found the action of wayfinding, stating that there are three stages: decision-
making, implementation, and processing of information. According to Evans (1980),
people learn about the environment from a map or during a journey. Therefore, when
people learn the environment from a map, they tend to develop form knowledge, but
when they learn the environment during a journey, they learn how to develop route
information (Nasar, 1988). Schmitz (1999) compiled all the information: in urban
wayfinding systems, the speed markers indicate the route markings, while the slow
ones use environmental signs. Naturally, the use of these environmental markers
relates to the correct perception of the environment. Individuals’ perception of the
environment depends on subjective information in their memories and their actions
onthisinformation(Andresenetal.,2016),becauseenvironmentalstructureinfluences
thestructureofperceptionandmemory;otherwise,theaccumulatedknowledgelevelis
very seldom used in movement and orientation behavior.
Inthis study,where asignificant numberofsubjectswasused inan unknownurban
fabric, the urban elements were shaped during the movement of direction towards a
target, the aim of which was to look at urban wayfinding behaviors from a perspective
different from that seen in the literature. The study examined the behavior of urban
design in wayfinding behaviors and the interactions of urban design with cognitive
and behavioral aspects in terms of neuro-cognitive aspects other than traditional
methods. The most important reason for this was to obtain more quantitative results
and to make concrete contributions to the design discipline according to said results.
Literature Review
The basic navigation strategy in people’s navigational behavior is goal-orientated and
aims to reach a destination with a specific target, such as minimizing travel distance
or time (Baldwin, 2009). Therefore, reaching the destination in the shortest time
through the most accurate route is the primary rule of proper wayfinding.
Pedestrian behaviors have been investigated for years using different systems and
methodologies.Greatprogresshasbeenmadeintheseinvestigationsfordecades.Infor-
mationrequirementsforpedestrianshavealsobeenexamined(May,2003),whileindoor

JOURNALOFURBANTECHNOLOGY 47
and outdoor pedestrian navigation systems have been discussed (Radoczky, 2007), cul-
turalheritagespaces(TolaciandKose,2021)andevenpreferencesinpedestriannaviga-
tion systems have been investigated (Li, 2006; Erkan, 2017). Studies that investigate the
wayfindingbehavioranalyzepeople’sbehaviorsduringawayfindingactfromasociologi-
cal, physical, and psychological perspective. Sanoff (2016) stated that the process of
wayfinding directions is a cognitive process that allows people to know where they are
and where they are going, so that they can choose an appropriate direction.
Inthiscognitiveprocess,thepersonmoveswithinthespacetoperceivetheenviron-
ment. Spatial activities can only be resolved when moving in space (Hoogstad, 1990).
Humans sense the details around them by moving their head, eyes, and body, and the
number of details they can perceive increases as they gain experience (Leavitt, 1988).
This situation is determined by the movement in the city as well as in the space, and
the sensor receives various images added one after the other from the place it moves.
These images can be obtained when passing from room to room in a building, turning
the corner of a street, or entering a yard (Dede, 1997). Therefore, inter-field movement
plays an important role in the wayfinding process.
Many wayfinding studies have investigated the effects of the physical environment
(O’Neil, 1991; Robinson, 2005) on the orientation behavior of personal characteristics
(Liu, 2011) and sign elements (Cheng, 2009; Roberts, 2009). Besides these, certain
other aspects have also been investigated, namely route preferences at the decision
point (Conroy et al., 2003; Kuipers et al., 2003), topological relations (Haq and
Zimring, 2003), cognitive approaches (Diaz Wionczek, 2002; Erkan, 2021), and
gaining spatial information (Meilinger and Knauff, 2008). Furthermore, the majority
of the wayfinding studies have investigated how individuals find their way based on
two hypothetical wayfinding styles, namely route-based and map/survey-based (Foo
et al., 2005; Xia, 2008). These studies suggest that decisions and actions in finding
specific directions are associated with intersections and landscapes.
Furthermore, there are few studies (Fendley, 2009; King, 2014; Zomer et al., 2019)
whichfocusontheurbanwayfindingbehaviorsinlargemetropolises,whichfaceexces-
sive daily commuting behaviors and have intense stimuli. Although urban density is
known as an important feature for the attraction and readability of an environment,
its role as a determinant is unknown (Emo, 2012). In addition, studies involve
different theories, i.e. cognitive maps to pointers, and from different perspectives. In
his study, Erkan (2018) analyzed wayfinding behaviors in architectural spaces and
found a direct relationship with the wayfinding behaviors of ceiling height. In other
words, it has been found that, if there is a higher ceiling height in architectural spaces,
then people can find their way easier. Studies related to navigation systems in architec-
turalspaces(DarkenandPeterson,2014;LiandKlippel,2016;DosenandOstwald,2017;
Erkan, 2018) reveal the effect of spaces on human behavior.
Thebasisofurbanwayfindingsystemsarecognitiveprocessessuchasspacedetection
and route selection (Miller and Carlson, 2011; C.T. Lin et al., 2012). These symbolic
structures are easily identified and perceived by everyone. Naturally, there are studies
that reveal the importance of landmarks and symbolic structures for definitions of
human navigation (Brosset et al., 2008; Sarjakoski et al., 2012). Moreover, Bruns and
Chamberlain (2019) stated that the accuracy of landmark configuration is highly corre-
lated with scene recognition, regardless of the landmarks’ order.

Another important element of urban wayfinding systems is cognitive maps as archi-
tecturalinteriorspaces.Studieshaveshownthatpeoplefindtheirwayinthecityeasilyby
creatingacognitivemap(Golledge,2003;GolledgeandGarling,2003).Koutsoklenisand
Papadopoulos (2011a) stated that all people have cognitive maps, including visually
impairedindividuals(Papadopoulos,2004).Whenapersonwithdeepvisionimpairment
or blindness enters a region, cognitive mapping directly refers to environmental signs
(i.e. olfactory, auditory, and haptic) (Koutsoklenis and Papadopoulos, 2011b). Mon-
dschein et al. (2010) investigated the influence of mode choices on the formation of
different cognitive maps of Los Angeles.
Many studies have investigated wayfinding behavior and its relationship to more
common daily commute characteristics, mainly by examining the frequency of visits
to specific neighborhoods or areas (Piccardi et al., 2011; Cashdan et al., 2016). In some
research, however, the wayfinding behavior has been studied in terms of distances,
turns, or transverse intersections between alternatives, usually on the chosen route
(Hölscher et al., 2011; Furman et al., 2014).
Zhang (2017)introducedvisual suggestionsto ease human movementand transpor-
tationsystemsinwayfindingbehaviorsinurbanstreets.Erkan(2017)arguedthatpeople
aredirectedtodifferentpointswithspecificstimuliandthatthesestimuliaffecttheaction
of wayfinding direction. Wayfinding preferences are analyzed using verbal reports of
respondents,walkingordrivingalongapredefinedroute(Meilingeretal.,2014;Middle-
ton,2018).However,duetothelackofcomprehensivestudiesprovidingnumericaldata,
thesmallnumberofparticipants,anddifferentpreferencesinnavigationsystems,itisnot
yetclearwhichnavigationalstrategiesarepreferredindailycommutebehaviorinurban
environments, their relationship with navigational behaviors, and whether there are
differences. In addition, innovative studies focused on brain activity using brain
imaging tools (functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI), magnetoencephalogra-
phy(MEG),electroencephalography[EEG])haveinvestigatedsocio-demographicdiffer-
ences and percentage of finding shortcuts in navigation based on photographs (Epstein
etal.,2005),findingdirectioninamuseum(Janzenetal.,2008)andinatask-orientated
perspective (Furman et al., 2014). Although there are different studies on urban orien-
tation(Denisetal.,2007;Mantuanoetal.,2017;Gamacheetal.,2020),researchprojects
investigating neuro-cognitive aspects are very limited.
Materials and Methods
Thisstudyattemptstodrawconclusionsfromthecombinationofmanydisciplinesand
interaction of different methods of analysis.
Participants
Participatinginthestudywere358womenand354men.Theiragesrangedfrom21to57
(M=34; SD=11.7). All 712 participants were university graduates and were reminded
that products such as alcohol should not be taken the night before joining the exper-
iment. All respondents were selected from people who actively used their right hand.
This is because the Wii controller was calibrated for right-hand users. All participants
signed an informed consent form before participation, and subsequently completed

imental stages. All participants reached the end point starting from the end point.
Although the starting and ending points were fixed, urban navigation was allowed
withinacertainperiodoftime.However,duetothelimitationsofthesoftware,thenavi-
gation time of the participants was limited.
Urban Design Criteria
This study was designed as a simple city for analyzing people’s urban wayfinding beha-
viors.Firstly,theurbandesignprinciplesfrommanyresearcherswerereviewed.Thecity
design methodologies were examined to gain specific insights. One of the main sources
forurbandesign,Lynch(1960),introducedthetermimageability,andhencetheenviron-
menthastheabilitytotakeonaninfluentialaestheticqualityinurbandesign.Hereby,he
proposed nodes, paths, landmarks, districts, and edges as essential elements of urban
design.
Furthermore, Jacobs and Appleyard (1987) put forth some goals that should be
addressed to produce good urban configurations. They argued that it is possible to
realize an ideal urban environment by transferring the goals into the design.
Conducting studies on environmental behaviors, Kaplan et al. (1989) developed four
complementaryqualitiesthataffectpeople’svisualexperiencesinthelandscape,andinves-
tigatedtheirimpactonurbandesign.Thesearelegibility,mystery,coherence,andcomplex-
ity.Rapoport(1990)identified36characteristicsofasuccessfulurbanenvironment,nearly
allofwhicharerelatedtosizeandshape.Hedevelopedthebeliefthatanaestheticallysuc-
cessfulurbanenvironmentwouldhaveahighlevelofenclosureandnarrowness,complex
profiles, highly articulated surfaces, and enclosing elements, grouped under six categories.
Gehl (1996) stated that the size, shape, connections, and positioning of items within a
space, and the detailed design of those items, are important in determining the quality of
a public space. Smith et al. (1997) developed a similar list of features that urban environ-
ments should provide: connection, mobility, liveability, character, personal freedom, and
diversity. Moughtin (2007) listed the elements of the nine traditional design principles
thatdescribebeautifularchitectureinurbanspacesandstatedthattheaestheticdesignprin-
ciplesofthecityareasfollows:symmetry,scale,proportion,order,unity,balance,rhythm,
contrast, and harmony. Weber et al. (2008) proposed symmetry, homogeneity, scale, and
uniformityaskeydeterminantsintheaestheticevaluationofthebuiltenvironment.More-
over,Reed(2011)focusedontheimportanceofvisualtermsintheinterpretationofspaces
during the analysis of the design aesthetics of the urban environment. The main com-
ponents of the environmental structure proposed by Reed (2011) include form, line,
color and texture. Nia and Atun (2016) stated that it is not only the specified elements
which are important in the aesthetic design of the city, but also the cognitive factors and
the factors that potentially stimulate people directly.

Considering the above-mentioned criteria, the city is designed with different sizes of

2. SecondArea(Purple-Zone):Thereareshoppingcentersandstoresinthisregion.The

3. Third Area (Yellow-Zone): This area can be defined as the area where human-scale

With this software, it was determined how long the participants spent in the city. In

Results
The city is divided into six different regions for accurate analysis. There are sculptures
and terraces designed accordingto different scales,as wellas greenareas and industrial
structures. The time participants spent from the starting point to the end point was
noted. With the UAT software, it was determined how much time participants spent
in the city. In the study, women completed the action of wayfinding in an average of
503.85 seconds; for the men, this time fell to 415.26 seconds. The density of the time
spent by urban area and participant is shown in Figure 4.
As seen in Figure 4,thereare differencesin navigations in thedesigned regions.It is
noteworthy that women spend more time wayfinding, and this is seen in all regions.
However, the difference between the wayfinding time of women and men is smallest
in the green region; the biggest difference is in the purple region. Behaviorally, men
spend more time in green areas, while it has been confirmed that women spend more
time in areas where shopping centers are located.

Landmark Analysis
In this study, the behaviors of the participants were examined in terms of landmarks
within the city. It is noteworthy that the participants differ in their EEG gamma waves
duringwayfindingaction.Anincreaseingammabandswasobservedastheparticipants

Discussion
Thisstudyanalyzedthewayfindingbehaviorofpeopleintheurbanenvironment.These
analysesweredividedintodifferentcategories.Themostimportantreasonfortheseana-
lyses is to determine the relationship between the factors that are thought to affect
wayfinding behaviors.
In the study, different brain responses were recorded in different urban areas with
different characteristics. At the same time, ET data were examined. With the UAT, the
time spent by the participants in the urban environment was determined, as were the
walkingroutesoftheparticipants.Inthestudy,itwasdeterminedthatlowbetaactivity
increased in most of the participants walking on narrow streets. Previous studies have
shownthatbetaactivityincreasesasafunctionofalertnessandvisualattention(Busch-
man and Miller, 2007; Dehzangi and Williams, 2015; Erkan, 2018). The increased
demands for attention and alertness required for navigating narrow streets can be
explainedbytheincreaseinlowbetawhenwalkingcomparedtowalkingonwidestreets.
Yang et al. (2011) stated that foliage such as small ornamental trees and shrubs can
reduce beta activity levels. This may explain the low beta level seen in the green field
environment of our study, in participants wandering in the so-called green-zone, com-
pared to the response to the absence of any vegetation in the so-called blue-zone,
wherethereisalmostnogreencover.Recentstudieshavereportedthatfamiliarenviron-
ments are associated with increases in alpha activity when viewing street scenes (Kacha
et al., 2015), and this effect is demonstrated by familiar motor action (Di Nota et al.,
2017). Alpha activities were observed intensely in people who see familiar chain cafes
(Starbucks) and markets (migros), especially in the orange-zone area where cafes are
dense,andespeciallyamongpeoplewithhighheatmapdensitiesinthesefamiliarareas.
AccordingtoBelingradandPeruch(2000),distinguishingpoints(landmarks,triangu-
lation points) are noteworthy in the spatial scale and support direction finding. Bruns
and Chamberlain (2019) stated that landmark objects assist in learning a route. This
studyalsoshowsthatlandmarksarethedesignelementsthatsupportwayfindingaction.

Previousstudieshavereportedthatalphawavesoccurinapersoninarestingstate,such
asconcentratedmeditationandrelaxing(Jangetal.,2014).Itisextremelyinterestingthat
the high and low buildings have different effects on the alpha relative strength. Specifi-
cally, the amplitudes were consistently higher when participants saw the low building
rather than the high building. Notably, increases in alpha wave activity have also been
associated with an improved perception of calmness (Palva and Palva, 2007) and
highly correlated with lower stress levels (Sowndhararajan and Kim, 2016). Alpha

quencyhasbeenreportedtobehighlycorrelatedwithcognitiveperformance(Klimesch
et al., 1993). Looking at the low building increased the relative strength of the alpha,
suggesting increased inner attention (Takahashi et al., 2005).
Conclusion
Thisstudyanalyzedurbanwayfindingbehaviorsinawaydifferentfromthatemployedin
traditional methods. Different techniques (EEG, ET, and VR) were planned to gather
from participants numerical data related to wayfinding. This study researched how
urban environment navigation was determined, while the effect of urban design on the
wayfinding behavior of people was questioned, and some critical points were pointed
out. These points are thought to contribute to urban design criteria:
1. People find their way more easily in wide streets than in narrow streets. EEG data
showed that low beta activity decreased in wide streets; therefore, stress factors are
thought to decrease in such streets. In addition, when ET data were examined, the
highestnumberofgazesandfixationswasrecordedduringnavigationinwidestreets;
2. Itwasdeterminedthatlandmarksareimportantdesignelementsinfindingdirection
inurbanenvironments.Interestingly,itwasobservedthatthegammabandincreased
in the seconds when participants saw the landmark. In this case, it is thought that
object recognition is provided, and so landmarks have a positive effect.
3. Structures with two different geometries were examined. When the high alpha/beta
values were examined, it was remarkable that the areas with amorphous geometry
hadhighervaluesthantheareaswithnormalgeometry.Consideringthattheincrease
